video_title: The Counterintuitive Rule That Could Beat the Market
gist: Despite the generic title, this is a financial-history interview: Meb Faber talks with Pulitzer-winning author Liaquat Ahamed about his book '1873: The Rothschilds, The First Great Depression and the Making of the Modern World.' Ahamed argues the 1873 bust was survivable but was turned into a 20-year deflation by a monetary policy error (Europe dumping silver for gold, shrinking the supply of the safe asset), and that the resulting debtor backlash produced populism, conspiracy theories and 20 years of political stalemate. His single modern worry is not US debt but a US stock market at ~$80 trillion versus ~$30 trillion of GDP, held by a 401(k)-era public with no bonds and a taste for speculation.

themes.theme: First Globalization: Railroads as the Single Driver

insights.claim: The 1850s-1873 expansion was the first true era of globalization: world trade grew fivefold and rose 2.5x as a share of GDP, funded by British and French capital exported into global infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Establishes the base rate for capital-export booms: cross-border funding of a single asset class can double trade intensity before it breaks, so watch the funding source, not just the asset.

insights.claim: The pre-1873 boom was uniquely concentrated: one technology (railroads) financed by one source (globally mobile European capital) drove the world economy, with railroad booms simultaneously in the US, Europe and even Argentina.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A single-factor, single-funding-source boom is the historical template for today's AI capex cycle; concentration in both the technology and its financing is what makes the unwind systemic rather than sectoral.
insights.quote: So, it was the first era in which a single factor, the railroads, and a single source, global capital, was driving the economy.

insights.claim: European capital supplied roughly one third of all money that went into US railroads, making the US an emerging market dependent on foreign portfolio flows before 1873.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Explains the transmission channel: when European credit froze, US infrastructure finance stopped regardless of US fundamentals - the same foreign-funding dependency to monitor in today's EM and capex-heavy credit.

themes.theme: A Bond-Only Saver Class and the Rothschild Underwriting Duopoly

insights.claim: The boom was funded by bonds, not equities, because a new European upper-middle-class saver class had been scarred by the deepest bear market they had experienced (roughly 1845 to 1850) and shunned stocks entirely.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Generational risk aversion redirects capital rather than removing it - a cohort scarred in one asset class will crowd into the 'safe' one and create the next bubble there instead.

insights.claim: Low yields pushed European savers into reach-for-yield behaviour: British gilts paid only 3% and French government bonds only 4%, so savers hunted abroad for more attractive investments.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The oldest driver of bad credit decisions is a 3-4% domestic risk-free rate; low real yields, not fraud, are what route savings into railroads, Egypt and Turkey.

insights.claim: The Rothschilds effectively invented and then dominated the global bond market, and after 1850 they plus Barings accounted for 70% of global bond issuance as underwriters.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A two-firm, 70%-share gatekeeper structure in primary credit markets is a systemic concentration - useful precedent when assessing today's concentration in private credit origination and index gatekeeping.
insights.quote: the masters of the universe in that era were the Rothschilds

themes.theme: Reparations Shock and the Gründerzeit IPO Mania

insights.claim: France's defeat in the 1870 Franco-Prussian War produced a $1 billion reparations payment (roughly $1 trillion in today's money using a 1,000x multiplier) injected into a German economy of only $4-5 billion over two years - about 20% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A 20%-of-GDP liquidity injection over two years is a quantifiable bubble trigger; the size and speed of a capital inflow, not its legitimacy, is what causes the asset mania.

insights.claim: The German bubble's mechanism was forced portfolio rotation: German states used the reparations money to retire all their government bonds, leaving conservative bondholders in Hamburg, Munich and Berlin holding cash with nowhere to go but equities for the first time in their lives.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Debt retirement is a bullish equity shock - when the safe-asset supply is withdrawn, savers are pushed up the risk curve, a mechanism to watch whenever governments or companies shrink bond supply.

insights.claim: The Gründerzeit ('founders era') was a two-to-three-year wave of IPOs across Germany, mostly banks and railroads, and Ahamed calls it the first IPO bubble, explicitly analogous to the 1990s dot-com bubble.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Supply of new issuance is the tell: charlatans form companies to absorb inflows, so IPO volume surging into a retail bid is a late-cycle marker rather than a sign of health.
insights.quote: Truly was the first IPO bubble. A little like the dot-com bubble of the 1990s.

themes.theme: Bimetallism, the Crime of '73 and the Safe-Asset Squeeze

insights.claim: France, not Britain, was the linchpin of the pre-1873 global financial system: it held the world's largest stock of both gold and silver, and the Banque de France acted as a balancing wheel, absorbing whichever metal was being over-mined and issuing currency against the other.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Identifies the hidden shock absorber in the system - and its removal as the real fragility; today's equivalent question is which balance sheet is quietly arbitraging the safe asset and what happens if it stops.
insights.quote: The Banque de France acted as a balancing wheel.

insights.claim: The US decision to return to metal by 1879 omitted silver almost accidentally, on the belief that Californian and other gold discoveries meant the world could dispense with silver entirely and run on gold alone.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A monetary regime's most damaging feature can be an unexamined assumption about future supply of the reserve asset - an error of omission, not a deliberate tightening.
insights.quote: there was a belief that there was so much gold in the world that the world would dispense with silver and just power the world economy on the basis of gold

insights.claim: Bismarck weaponised monetary policy after winning the Franco-Prussian War by selling all of Germany's silver for gold, collapsing the silver price, damaging Germany but damaging France far more and triggering a Europe-wide abandonment of silver.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A precedent for deliberate financial warfare against a rival's monetary base, with self-inflicted damage accepted as the cost - relevant to how reserve-asset weaponisation propagates today.

insights.claim: The deflation's proximate cause was a safe-asset shortage: in a crisis everyone scrambles for precious metals, but with silver collapsing the entire scramble concentrated on gold, tightening credit so hard that wholesale prices fell 30% in 1873 and kept falling for 20 years.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Quantifies the core lesson: shrinking the supply of the safe asset during a flight to quality converts a bust into a depression - a template for watching collateral scarcity in modern crises.
insights.quote: in 173, prices wholesale prices fall by 30% by the end of the year. And that is the beginning of a 20-year deflation in prices.

insights.claim: The crisis unfolded in three separated stages that lulled investors: Central European stocks crashed first (major Vienna and German names fell 50% in a single day), then nothing happened and everyone concluded Vienna was simply overpriced, before the New York leg hit in September.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The false-all-clear between crisis legs is the dangerous window; a first shock that fails to propagate immediately is not evidence of containment.

insights.claim: The September 1873 New York leg was a credit event rather than an equity event, triggered when Jay Cooke and Company - the premier US investment bank, which had raised $2 billion for the Union during the Civil War and was a friend of the president - announced it could no longer finance its sponsored railroad.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The failure of the most connected, highest-status financier is the psychological trigger that repices everyone else's funding access - explicitly the Lehman analogue.
insights.quote: In the same way that when Lehman went under, it had a massive psychological effect.

insights.claim: The railroad default cascade was severe and slow-burning: a third of US railroad companies had stopped paying interest by the end of 1873, and half had stopped within five years.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Gives a realistic default-severity benchmark for a single-sector capex bubble financed with foreign debt: roughly 33% impaired in year one, 50% by year five.
insights.quote: By the end of the year, a third of the railroad companies had stopped paying interest. Within 5 years, half the railroad companies had stopped paying interest in the US.

insights.claim: The final leg was emerging-market sovereign default: Egypt and Turkey had together borrowed about $1.5 billion on the London Stock Exchange - roughly the same as all US railroads - on prospects Ahamed calls laughable in hindsight, and both defaulted.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: When a yield-starved saver base is bidding, the marginal borrower's story quality collapses - EM sovereign issuance at par with the era's flagship growth sector is a late-cycle warning.

themes.theme: Deflation's Debtor Backlash: Farmers, Bailouts and Scapegoats

insights.claim: Deflation is symmetrically hated to inflation because it redistributes rather than merely lowers prices: owners of financial assets benefit while mortgage holders, farmers and indebted households see their debts become a millstone.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A clean allocation map for a deflationary regime: long financial assets and creditors, short leveraged real-asset owners - and expect the political backlash to come from the second group.
insights.quote: suddenly your goods are cheaper but your debts start accumulating. And what you borrowed acts like this giant millstone on your back.

insights.claim: Japan after 1990 is the living case study Ahamed uses: a house bought with a mortgage was worth half as much 30 years later while the mortgage remained, which suppressed investment capacity and produced three lost decades.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The mechanism by which deflation kills growth is balance-sheet-constrained investment, not weak demand alone - the thing to monitor is debtor capacity to invest, not just the price level.

insights.claim: Deflation split the US along a new geographic-economic fault line - western farmers against eastern bankers - which fractured both the Republican and Democratic parties and produced roughly 20 years of political stalemate.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Monetary regimes generate durable political realignments; a two-decade price shock produced two decades of governing paralysis, a policy-risk horizon worth pricing.

insights.claim: Ahamed's core critique of 2008 is asymmetry, not intervention: bailing out the banks was exactly the right thing to do, but not bailing out homeowners created the grievance that fragmented the Democratic Party and produced both Bernie Sanders' left and the Tea Party right.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The political cost of a crisis response depends on who is left holding the debt, not the size of the rescue - a forward-looking constraint on how the next bailout can be structured.
insights.quote: The problem was they didn't bail out the homeowners.

insights.claim: Prolonged debtor distress is fertile ground for conspiracy theories and scapegoating, which after 1873 took the form of an economically motivated (rather than religious) anti-Semitism in Europe, and in the US produced the 'crime of '73' myth that British bankers and the Rothschilds bribed Congress to abandon silver - stories Ahamed says were entirely bogus.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Scapegoat narratives are a predictable output of long deflations, and they attach to the most visible financial intermediary - a reputational and regulatory risk factor for whoever is the era's 'master of the universe'.
insights.quote: it was a different form of anti-Semitism. Before then it had been religious. This time it was economic.

themes.theme: The Policy Dilemma: Safe-Asset Demand vs Inflation Discipline

insights.claim: Ahamed's synthesis across both his books is that the economy was surprisingly resilient to the 1873 boom-bust, and it was the monetary error - abandoning silver for gold - that turned a bust into the first great depression, mirroring how staying on gold after WWI created the money shortage behind the 1930s.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Reframes depression risk as a policy-error variable rather than a bubble-size variable: the size of the bust matters less than whether the monetary response shrinks or expands the safe asset.
insights.quote: the economy was surprisingly resilient. And what really caused the bust to turn into the first great depression was this giant monetary mistake of abandoning silver and going on to the gold standard.

insights.claim: The transferable dilemma is that a crisis creates demand for safe assets that only the government or central bank can supply, but if that authority has already allowed inflation to take off it must choose between fighting inflation and satisfying the liquidity scramble - damned either way.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The single most actionable modern read-through: a Fed entering a market break with unfinished inflation business has no clean option, which widens the distribution of policy outcomes.

insights.claim: Ahamed signals that he would not want to be in the central bank chair's position if there is a stock market stumble from current levels - a hedged but pointed statement of the policy bind ahead.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The guest's clearest implied view: the next equity drawdown arrives with the monetary authority constrained, so expect a slower or messier policy response than markets assume.
insights.quote: And I think, you know, I would not like to be in Chairman Volcker's shoes if we get a stock market stumble.

themes.theme: Today's Fragility: $80T Equity Market vs $30T GDP

insights.claim: Ahamed's stated top risk is the stock market rather than the debt: the US equity market is about $80 trillion against roughly $30 trillion of GDP, more than 250% of GDP, versus a brief peak of maybe 120% in 2000.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable valuation anchor and an explicit rejection of the consensus debt-crisis framing - the transmission channel to worry about is the wealth effect, not the deficit.
insights.quote: The US stock market is now $80 trillion in a GDP of $30 trillion. That is more than 250% of GDP. We've never been here.

insights.claim: The 401(k) system has produced an all-equity household allocation with no perceived role for bonds - Ahamed notes his own children, in their early 40s, hold their entire 401(k)s in equities and see no reason to own a bond.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Structural, price-insensitive equity demand is also structural fragility: a cohort with no bond allocation has no shock absorber, and behaviour on the first real drawdown is untested.
insights.quote: My kids are in their early 40s, and they have all of their 401(k)s are in equities, and they see no reason to own a bond.

insights.claim: The public has developed a durable taste for speculation, evidenced by successive bubbles in meme stocks, crypto and gold, with everyone hunting for something that will go up ten times.
insights.speaker: Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: Serial speculative episodes across unrelated assets indicate a behavioural regime rather than isolated manias - a sentiment condition that tends to precede the terminal phase of a boom.
insights.quote: So, everyone's looking for something that's going to go up 10 times.

insights.claim: Faber's behavioural point is that in every cycle investors believe they can exit before the party ends but nobody actually wants to leave, with the final phase feeling like an accelerant - to which Ahamed counters with J.P. Morgan's stated secret of success: selling too early.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber and Liaquat Ahamed
insights.so_what: The only practical exit discipline offered in the episode: accept underperformance from selling early rather than relying on an ability to time the top that history says nobody exercises.
insights.quote: They once asked him, "What's the secret to your success?" And he said, "Selling too early."
